title: Judges 9:1–6
context: After Gideon’s death, his son Abimelech, born to a concubine from Shechem (8:31), seeks power through his mother’s family. He asks the Shechemites whether they prefer the rule of seventy brothers or of one man who is their own flesh. Funded with silver from the temple of Baal Berith, he hires reckless men and kills his seventy brothers on one stone at Ophrah; only Jotham, the youngest, escapes. The men of Shechem make Abimelech king, a sharp turn from Gideon’s refusal of kingship in 8:22–23.

verses.text: Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother’s brothers, and spoke with them and with all the family of the house of his mother’s father, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech goes to his mother’s relatives in Shechem to build support. Arminian readers note that he exploits family ties for political gain, a deliberate choice that begins a chain of violence the chapter traces to its end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that his name can be read as “my father is king,” an irony given Gideon’s refusal of kingship (8:22–23). Shared ground: the verse opens a story of a son seeking the throne his father declined, by means God does not approve.

verses.text: “Please speak in the ears of all the men of Shechem, ‘Is it better for you that all the sons of Jerubbaal, who are seventy persons, rule over you, or that one rule over you?’ Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.”
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech frames the choice as seventy rulers versus one who is their own bone and flesh. Arminian readers see a manipulative appeal to kinship and self-interest, offered to people free to refuse but willing to listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the seventy sons ruling is Abimelech’s own framing, not something the text says Gideon arranged. Both traditions see the speech as political manipulation aimed at stirring tribal loyalty in Shechem.

verses.text: His mother’s brothers spoke of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem all these words. Their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech; for they said, “He is our brother.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Shechemites incline to Abimelech because he is their brother. Arminian readers stress that the men of Shechem make their own decision here, and the text will later hold them responsible for supporting him (9:24).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the heart’s inclination toward a kinsman reveals misplaced loyalty, valuing family ties above justice. Shared ground: the people’s choice is culpable, and the narrative will judge both Abimelech and those who backed him.

verses.text: They gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal Berith, with which Abimelech hired vain and reckless fellows who followed him.
verses.arminianNotes: They give him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal Berith, and he hires reckless men. Arminian readers note the link to 8:33, where Israel made Baal Berith their god, and see idolatry funding violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the dark irony of a god whose name relates to covenant financing covenant-breaking murder. Both traditions read the detail as showing how false worship and injustice are bound together in Shechem’s support for Abimelech.

verses.text: He went to his father’s house at Ophrah, and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, being seventy persons, on one stone; but Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.
verses.arminianNotes: Abimelech kills his seventy brothers on one stone at Ophrah, and only Jotham escapes by hiding. Arminian readers state the act plainly as fratricide, a grave crime against his own father’s house committed by deliberate choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the killing on one stone as a grim, almost ritual execution, and note that God preserves one witness, Jotham. Shared ground: the text presents the massacre as wickedness that God will repay (9:56).

verses.text: All the men of Shechem assembled themselves together with all the house of Millo, and went and made Abimelech king by the oak of the pillar that was in Shechem.
verses.arminianNotes: Shechem and the house of Millo make Abimelech king by the oak of the pillar. Arminian readers note that this site may recall earlier covenant scenes at Shechem (Joshua 24:26), now used to crown a murderer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the coronation as Israel’s first attempt at kingship carried out apart from God’s call. The identity of the house of Millo is uncertain. Both traditions read the scene as a sobering contrast with God’s rule that Gideon had affirmed.
